query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

cited_evidence.text: Multi-component alloys containing Co, Cr, Ni and other elements have attracted attention recently []. Equiatomic CoCrNi MEAs in particular demonstrate high strength and ductility at low temperatures []. CoCrNi MEAs are typically manufactured by casting and powder metallurgy, yielding a room temperature yield strength of only 360 MPa. Higher mechanical properties require additional processing like rolling, heat treatment and high pressure torsion []. Mechanical alloying (MA) combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS) can also produce CoCrNi MEAs with improved mechanics []. Traditional casting has some shortcomings such as low solidification rate, element segregation and rough casting microstructure, which requires heat treatment to optimize the structure. Compared to traditional casting, LAM can fabricate complex geometries []. LAM enables high cooling rates and temperature gradients, yielding refined solid solution phases and microstructures well-suited for high quality CoCrNi MEAs. Research on CoCrNi MEAs with LAM remains limited. There are many articles on LAM of CoCrNi MEAs. but there are very few articles on HSLAM CoCrNi MEAs. Additive manufacturing (AM) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal technology for industrial part production due to its ability to create intricate shapes through computer-assisted layer-by-layer part construction. In metal AM, a broad, ever-expanding technology landscape has emerged with varying degrees of adoption in industry. While various AM technologies exist, liquid-mediated metal AM, notably Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), has garnered significant interest in industry and academia due to its potential to produce high-quality parts. L-PBF’s quality relies on understanding the interplay between process parameters, material properties, and solidification conditions. Traditional alloy design primarily targets specific manufacturing routes and often overlooks the unique demands of additive manufacturing (AM). In AM, designing alloys requires optimizing both chemistry and processing conditions simultaneously to minimize defects and enhance reliability. Conventional approaches first focus on achieving target properties and then on developing scalable processing methods. Manufacturing processes have a strong influence on the mechanical properties of HEAs. It has been determined that the CoCrFeNi part produced by the hot-rolling process has a better yield and ultimate strength compared to the casted parts [,,,]. Additive manufacturing processes, such as Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), can improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys due to their inherent unique processing characteristics. Specifically, the rapid solidification and repeated remelting associated with these techniques facilitate the formation of fine grains and numerous substructures with a high density of dislocations, thereby enhancing the yield strength compared to conventionally processed alloys. Brif et al. [] showed that the yield strength of the CoCrFeNi alloy produced by the powder bed fusion (PBF) process is twice, respectively, the treble of that alloy in as-cast condition, and Kuzminova [] showed in turn that the yield strength of alloys using L-PBF is twice than that of hot-rolled alloys. However, the thermal cycling and partial remelting experienced by previous layers can significantly increase the hot cracking susceptibility of superalloys [].
